claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest living relatives of animals.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying animal multicellularity evolved, in part, through the modification of ancient adhesion and signaling pathways found in the unicellular and colonial progenitors of animals. The evolution of the animal molecular toolkit may be reconstructed through the study of the choanoflagellates, the closest living relatives of animals (Lang et al., 2002; Carr et al., 2008; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Philippe et al., 2009; Paps et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published phylogenetic studies establishing the evolutionary relationship between choanoflagellates and animals.

claim: Choanoflagellates express diverse genes required for animal multicellularity, including C-type lectins, cadherins, and tyrosine kinases.
source: For example, despite the fact that choanoflagellates are not animals, they express diverse genes required for animal multicellularity, including C-type lectins, cadherins, and tyrosine kinases (Abedin and King, 2008; King et al., 2008; Manning et al., 2008; Nichols et al., 2012; Suga et al., 2012; Fairclough et al., 2013), demonstrating that these genes predate the origin of animals.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting the presence of these gene families in choanoflagellates.

claim: These genes (C-type lectins, cadherins, and tyrosine kinases) predate the origin of animals.
source: For example, despite the fact that choanoflagellates are not animals, they express diverse genes required for animal multicellularity, including C-type lectins, cadherins, and tyrosine kinases (Abedin and King, 2008; King et al., 2008; Manning et al., 2008; Nichols et al., 2012; Suga et al., 2012; Fairclough et al., 2013), demonstrating that these genes predate the origin of animals.
evidence: Inference based on the presence of these genes in choanoflagellates, which are the closest living relatives of animals and diverged before the origin of animals.

claim: Single cells of S. rosetta undergo serial rounds of cell division to develop into spherical rosette colonies.
source: Through a process that resembles the earliest stages of embryogenesis in marine invertebrates, single cells of S. rosetta undergo serial rounds of cell division to develop into spherical rosette colonies (hereafter, 'rosettes'; Figure 1) (Fairclough et al., 2010; Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and reference to Figure 1 showing rosette morphology.

claim: Rosette development in S. rosetta resembles the earliest stages of embryogenesis in marine invertebrates.
source: Through a process that resembles the earliest stages of embryogenesis in marine invertebrates, single cells of S. rosetta undergo serial rounds of cell division to develop into spherical rosette colonies (hereafter, 'rosettes'; Figure 1) (Fairclough et al., 2010; Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies describing the developmental process.

claim: The switch between the S. rosetta solitary life style and rosette development is regulated by specific lipids produced by the prey bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis.
source: Importantly, the switch between the S. rosetta solitary life style and rosette development is regulated by specific lipids produced by the prey bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis (Alegado et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study demonstrating bacterial regulation of rosette development.

claim: The genome and transcriptome of S. rosetta have been sequenced and analyzed.
source: Moreover, the genome and transcriptome of S. rosetta have been sequenced and analyzed, revealing numerous homologs of diverse animal genes, many of which are up-regulated in colonies (Fairclough et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to the genome sequencing study.

claim: Numerous homologs of diverse animal genes are present in S. rosetta, many of which are up-regulated in colonies.
source: Moreover, the genome and transcriptome of S. rosetta have been sequenced and analyzed, revealing numerous homologs of diverse animal genes, many of which are up-regulated in colonies (Fairclough et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to the genome and transcriptome analysis.

claim: S. rosetta can be induced to undergo sex and meiosis.
source: We recently found that S. rosetta can be induced to undergo sex and meiosis, suggesting that it may be amenable to mapping crosses (Levin and King, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Haploid S. rosetta cells were exposed to 0.3% EMS or 6300 rems X-rays for mutagenesis.
source: To induce mutations in S. rosetta, cultures of haploid cells were exposed either to 0.3% EMS or 6300 rems X-rays, which resulted in a 10% or 40% reduction in cell number, respectively, when averaged across multiple trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental procedure described in the text with reference to data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Exposure to 0.3% EMS resulted in a 10% reduction in cell number.
source: To induce mutations in S. rosetta, cultures of haploid cells were exposed either to 0.3% EMS or 6300 rems X-rays, which resulted in a 10% or 40% reduction in cell number, respectively, when averaged across multiple trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from mutagenesis trials shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Exposure to 6300 rems X-rays resulted in a 40% reduction in cell number.
source: To induce mutations in S. rosetta, cultures of haploid cells were exposed either to 0.3% EMS or 6300 rems X-rays, which resulted in a 10% or 40% reduction in cell number, respectively, when averaged across multiple trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from mutagenesis trials shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 15,344 clonal cultures were screened for the presence or absence of rosettes.
source: We screened 15,344 clonal cultures for the presence or absence of rosettes (Figure 2).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of cultures screened in the forward genetic screen.

claim: Nine mutants with validated rosette defects were isolated.
source: Nine mutants with validated rosette defects were isolated ('Materials and methods'), each of which showed a significant reduction in rosette development relative to wild type (Figure 3A).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of mutants isolated, with reference to data in Figure 3A.

claim: Each of the nine rosette defect mutants showed a significant reduction in rosette development relative to wild type.
source: Nine mutants with validated rosette defects were isolated ('Materials and methods'), each of which showed a significant reduction in rosette development relative to wild type (Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating reduced rosette formation in mutants.

claim: The nine rosette defect mutants fell into seven phenotypic classes (classes A–G).
source: The nine rosette defect mutants fell into seven phenotypic classes (classes A–G, Table 1; Figure 3) based upon their ability to form rosette colonies in the presence of ACM or live A. machipongonensis, their swimming behavior as solitary cells, and the morphology of chain colonies produced when grown in the absence of ACM.
evidence: Classification based on multiple phenotypic criteria described in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Rosetteless cells failed entirely to develop into rosettes in the presence of either ACM or live A. machipongonensis.
source: Class A consisted of a single mutant, named Rosetteless, that was isolated after EMS treatment. In the presence of either ACM or live A. machipongonensis, Rosetteless cells failed entirely to develop into rosettes, but their cell morphology and proliferation were otherwise indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Phenotypic characterization shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rosetteless cell morphology and proliferation were otherwise indistinguishable from wild type.
source: Class A consisted of a single mutant, named Rosetteless, that was isolated after EMS treatment. In the presence of either ACM or live A. machipongonensis, Rosetteless cells failed entirely to develop into rosettes, but their cell morphology and proliferation were otherwise indistinguishable from wild type (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Growth curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrating normal proliferation.

claim: Rosetteless was isolated after EMS treatment.
source: Class A consisted of a single mutant, named Rosetteless, that was isolated after EMS treatment.
evidence: Direct statement of the mutagenesis method used to isolate Rosetteless.

claim: After filtering sequence variants by quality, 25,160 potential genetic markers were identified that differed between Rosetteless and the reference genome sequence.
source: After filtering the sequence variants by quality, we identified 25,160 potential genetic markers that differed between Rosetteless and the reference genome sequence, only four of which were unique to the Rosetteless genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Genome sequencing and variant calling data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only four sequence variants were unique to the Rosetteless genome.
source: After filtering the sequence variants by quality, we identified 25,160 potential genetic markers that differed between Rosetteless and the reference genome sequence, only four of which were unique to the Rosetteless genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Variant analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rosetteless was mated with Isolate B, which carried 39,451 putative sequence polymorphisms relative to Rosetteless.
source: To this end, Rosetteless was mated with another, previously sequenced S. rosetta strain, Isolate B (Levin and King, 2013), that carried 39,451 putative sequence polymorphisms relative to Rosetteless (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Genome comparison data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Seven outcrossed diploids were isolated and established as clonal cultures.
source: Using a combination of serial dilutions and genotyping, we isolated seven outcrossed diploids and established clonal cultures (Figure 4, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Experimental procedure and results described in the text and Figure 4.

claim: Of 442 clonal cultures genotyped, 182 were haploid progeny of the cross.
source: Of 442 clonal cultures genotyped, 182 were haploid progeny of the cross, as evidenced by their homozygosity at three microsatellite markers ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Genotyping data from the mapping cross.

claim: Only one mutation (supercontig 8, position 427,804) was tightly linked (<0.56 cM) to the rosette defect phenotype.
source: Most importantly, the genotype data revealed only one mutation (supercontig 8, position 427,804) that was tightly linked (<0.56 cM) to the rosette defect phenotype.
evidence: Linkage analysis from the mapping cross genotyping data.

claim: The mutation at supercontig 8, position 427,804 was linked to the Rosetteless phenotype in all examined haploid progeny from the Rosetteless × Isolate B cross (177/177).
source: The presence of the mutation was linked to the presence of the Rosetteless phenotype in all examined haploid progeny from the Rosetteless × Isolate B cross (177/177, Figure 4).
evidence: Perfect linkage data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating 177/177 progeny with concordant genotype and phenotype.

claim: The mutation at supercontig 8, position 427,804 disrupts a splice donor in the gene EGD82922.
source: Moreover, the mutation was one of the four validated Rosetteless-specific SNVs and, by disrupting a splice donor in the gene EGD82922, was the only one predicted to cause a coding change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Sequence analysis and variant annotation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mutation at supercontig 8, position 427,804 was the only one predicted to cause a coding change among the four validated Rosetteless-specific SNVs.
source: Moreover, the mutation was one of the four validated Rosetteless-specific SNVs and, by disrupting a splice donor in the gene EGD82922, was the only one predicted to cause a coding change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Variant annotation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The candidate splice donor mutation in the gene EGD82922 is responsible for the rosette defect phenotype.
source: Therefore, based on the tight linkage between the EDG82922 mutation and the phenotype, as well as the absence of any other detected polymorphisms in the 5′ end of supercontig 8, we infer that the candidate splice donor mutation in the gene EGD82922 is responsible for the rosette defect phenotype.
evidence: Inference based on tight genetic linkage and absence of other candidate mutations.

claim: The rtls gene encodes a 119 kDa protein with an N-terminal signal peptide and two C-type lectin-like domains (CTLDs).
source: The rtls gene encodes a 119 kDa protein with an N-terminal signal peptide and two C-type lectin-like domains (CTLDs; Figure 5A).
evidence: Protein domain analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CTLD-containing proteins are found in all animal lineages.
source: CTLD-containing proteins, including the C-type lectins, are found in all animal lineages and play diverse roles, including cell–cell adhesion, cell–extracellular matrix adhesion, cell signaling, and innate immune recognition of pathogens through their binding to carbohydrates, proteoglycans, lipids, and other ligands (Ruoslahti, 1996; Cambi et al., 2005; Zelensky and Gready, 2005; Geijtenbeek and Gringhuis, 2009; Švajger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on CTLD-containing proteins.

claim: CTLD-containing proteins play diverse roles, including cell–cell adhesion, cell–extracellular matrix adhesion, cell signaling, and innate immune recognition of pathogens.
source: CTLD-containing proteins, including the C-type lectins, are found in all animal lineages and play diverse roles, including cell–cell adhesion, cell–extracellular matrix adhesion, cell signaling, and innate immune recognition of pathogens through their binding to carbohydrates, proteoglycans, lipids, and other ligands (Ruoslahti, 1996; Cambi et al., 2005; Zelensky and Gready, 2005; Geijtenbeek and Gringhuis, 2009; Švajger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on CTLD protein functions.

claim: The Rtls CTLDs contain four conserved cysteines required for two disulfide bonds.
source: Similar to CTLDs from animals, the Rtls CTLDs contain four conserved cysteines required for two disulfide bonds, as well as the Glu-Pro-Asn motif (Figure 5B) that is required for mannose binding in some C-type lectins (Drickamer, 1992).
evidence: Sequence alignment shown in Figure 5B demonstrating conserved cysteines.

claim: The Rtls CTLDs contain the Glu-Pro-Asn motif that is required for mannose binding in some C-type lectins.
source: Similar to CTLDs from animals, the Rtls CTLDs contain four conserved cysteines required for two disulfide bonds, as well as the Glu-Pro-Asn motif (Figure 5B) that is required for mannose binding in some C-type lectins (Drickamer, 1992).
evidence: Sequence alignment shown in Figure 5B and citation to literature on mannose-binding motifs.

claim: Rtls contains several low-complexity regions that each consists of as many as 50–60 consecutive threonines and serines.
source: Rtls also contains several low-complexity regions that each consists of as many as 50–60 consecutive threonines and serines and two high-complexity internal repeat regions (RP1 and RP2) of unknown function near the C-terminus of the protein (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Protein sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: Rtls contains two high-complexity internal repeat regions (RP1 and RP2) of unknown function near the C-terminus of the protein.
source: Rtls also contains several low-complexity regions that each consists of as many as 50–60 consecutive threonines and serines and two high-complexity internal repeat regions (RP1 and RP2) of unknown function near the C-terminus of the protein (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Protein sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: The serine-threonine-rich regions resemble mucin-like domains found in some animal C-type lectins and are likely sites of O-linked glycosylation.
source: The serine-threonine-rich regions resemble mucin-like domains found in some animal C-type lectins and are likely sites of O-linked glycosylation (Carraway and Hull, 1991; Drickamer and Dodd, 1999).
evidence: Inference based on sequence similarity to known mucin-like domains, supported by citations.

claim: The rtlsl1 mutation is a T-to-C mutation in the predicted splice donor of intron 7.
source: The rtlsl1 mutation, a T-to-C mutation in the predicted splice donor of intron 7, falls 3′ of the sequences encoding the two CTLDs and 5′ of the RP1 and RP2 sequences (Figure 5A).
evidence: Mutation position and type shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The rtlsl1 mutation falls 3′ of the sequences encoding the two CTLDs and 5′ of the RP1 and RP2 sequences.
source: The rtlsl1 mutation, a T-to-C mutation in the predicted splice donor of intron 7, falls 3′ of the sequences encoding the two CTLDs and 5′ of the RP1 and RP2 sequences (Figure 5A).
evidence: Gene structure and mutation position shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Wild-type rtls is spliced as predicted in wild-type cells.
source: However, when using primers that could amplify either the wild-type isoform or variant splice isoforms (a 5′ primer bridging the exon 5/6 junction paired with a 3′ primer in exon 12), we found that rtls was spliced as predicted in wild-type cells, but produced multiple, variant splice isoforms in Rosetteless cells.
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: rtls produced multiple, variant splice isoforms in Rosetteless cells.
source: However, when using primers that could amplify either the wild-type isoform or variant splice isoforms (a 5′ primer bridging the exon 5/6 junction paired with a 3′ primer in exon 12), we found that rtls was spliced as predicted in wild-type cells, but produced multiple, variant splice isoforms in Rosetteless cells.
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D,E demonstrating multiple splice isoforms.

claim: The variant isoforms included one isoform in which intron 7 was retained.
source: The variant isoforms included one isoform in which intron 7 was retained and two smaller isoforms in which an alternative splice donor either 14 bp upstream or 27 bp downstream of the mutation was used instead (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The variant isoforms included two smaller isoforms in which an alternative splice donor either 14 bp upstream or 27 bp downstream of the mutation was used.
source: The variant isoforms included one isoform in which intron 7 was retained and two smaller isoforms in which an alternative splice donor either 14 bp upstream or 27 bp downstream of the mutation was used instead (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The wild-type rtls isoform was not detected in Rosetteless cells using RT-PCR with primers bridging the exon 5/6 junction and exon 12.
source: Importantly, the wild-type rtls isoform was not detected in Rosetteless cells using this assay.
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For two of the major splice isoforms in Rosetteless cells, the altered splicing led to frame shifts and early stop codons downstream of the mutation.
source: For two of the major splice isoforms in Rosetteless cells, the altered splicing led to frame shifts and early stop codons downstream of the mutation, which may either lead to a truncation of the Rtls protein or to degradation of the transcript by nonsense mediated decay in mutant cells (Lareau et al., 2007).
evidence: Sequence analysis shown in Figure 5E with stop codons indicated.

claim: Total Rtls protein levels in mutant cells were approximately 25% that of wild-type cells.
source: Using this antibody, we found that total Rtls protein levels in mutant cells were ∼25% that of wild-type cells (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Dot blot quantification data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Treatment with anti-Rtls resulted in significant inhibition of rosette formation relative to negative controls.
source: Treatment with anti-Rtls resulted in significant inhibition of rosette formation relative to negative controls (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating reduced rosette formation with antibody treatment.

claim: In cultures treated with 50 µg/ml anti-Rtls during rosette induction, only 10 ± 11% of cells were observed in rosettes.
source: Specifically, in cultures treated with 50 µg/ml anti-Rtls during rosette induction, only 10 ± 11% of cells were observed in rosettes (mean ± standard deviation, Figure 6A).
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Wild-type S. rosetta cultures incubated with pre-immune serum showed 91 ± 2% of cells in rosettes.
source: In contrast, wild-type S. rosetta cultures incubated with an equal volume of rabbit pre-immune serum or an equivalent concentration of normal rabbit IgG or BSA showed normal levels of rosette development, with 91 ± 2%, 90 ± 2%, or 88 ± 1% of cells in rosettes, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Wild-type S. rosetta cultures incubated with normal rabbit IgG showed 90 ± 2% of cells in rosettes.
source: In contrast, wild-type S. rosetta cultures incubated with an equal volume of rabbit pre-immune serum or an equivalent concentration of normal rabbit IgG or BSA showed normal levels of rosette development, with 91 ± 2%, 90 ± 2%, or 88 ± 1% of cells in rosettes, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Wild-type S. rosetta cultures incubated with BSA showed 88 ± 1% of cells in rosettes.
source: In contrast, wild-type S. rosetta cultures incubated with an equal volume of rabbit pre-immune serum or an equivalent concentration of normal rabbit IgG or BSA showed normal levels of rosette development, with 91 ± 2%, 90 ± 2%, or 88 ± 1% of cells in rosettes, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment of wild-type cells with 50 µg/ml anti-Rtls did not result in a loss of cell viability or reduction in cell growth.
source: Importantly, treatment of wild-type cells with 50 µg/ml anti-Rtls did not result in a loss of cell viability or reduction in cell growth (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Cell density data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The function of secreted Rtls is specific to and essential for rosette development.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the function of secreted Rtls is specific to and essential for rosette development.
evidence: Conclusion based on antibody blocking experiments showing specific inhibition of rosette development without affecting cell viability.

claim: In rosettes, Rtls was detected as a thick layer associated with the basal poles of the cells.
source: In wild-type cells, Rtls was highly enriched in the extracellular matrix-filled center of rosettes, where it was observed in a thick layer underlying the basal poles of all cells in the rosette (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Rtls was highly enriched in the extracellular matrix-filled center of rosettes.
source: In wild-type cells, Rtls was highly enriched in the extracellular matrix-filled center of rosettes, where it was observed in a thick layer underlying the basal poles of all cells in the rosette (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: In most instances, Rtls was observed to connect all but one pair of neighboring cells in rosettes.
source: While Rtls staining sometimes connected all cells in the center of rosettes (Figure 6C), in most instances Rtls was observed to connect all but one pair of neighboring cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Rosettes form through a process of incomplete cytokinesis.
source: Because rosettes form through a process of incomplete cytokinesis (Fairclough et al., 2010; Dayel et al., 2011), this discontinuous Rtls staining may reflect the history of cell division during rosette formation, with discontinuities in its distribution indicating adjacent cells that were not sisters.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on rosette development.

claim: Discontinuous Rtls staining may reflect the history of cell division during rosette formation, with discontinuities in its distribution indicating adjacent cells that were not sisters.
source: Because rosettes form through a process of incomplete cytokinesis (Fairclough et al., 2010; Dayel et al., 2011), this discontinuous Rtls staining may reflect the history of cell division during rosette formation, with discontinuities in its distribution indicating adjacent cells that were not sisters.
evidence: Speculation based on the pattern of Rtls staining and knowledge of rosette development.

claim: Rtls may regulate rosette development by interacting with components of the extracellular matrix (ECM).
source: We hypothesize that Rtls regulates rosette development by interacting with components of the extracellular matrix (ECM), which has previously been shown to fill the center of rosettes (Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: Hypothesis based on Rtls localization in the ECM-filled center of rosettes.

claim: The extracellular matrix has previously been shown to fill the center of rosettes.
source: We hypothesize that Rtls regulates rosette development by interacting with components of the extracellular matrix (ECM), which has previously been shown to fill the center of rosettes (Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Equivalent levels of Rtls were detected in lysates from rosette-induced and -uninduced cultures.
source: Despite the fact that equivalent levels of Rtls were detected in lysates from rosette-induced and -uninduced cultures (Figure 5F), little to no Rtls signal was detected by immunofluorescence when wild-type single cells and chains were imaged with the settings used for visualizing Rtls in rosettes (Figure 6C).
evidence: Dot blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Little to no Rtls signal was detected by immunofluorescence when wild-type single cells and chains were imaged with the settings used for visualizing Rtls in rosettes.
source: Despite the fact that equivalent levels of Rtls were detected in lysates from rosette-induced and -uninduced cultures (Figure 5F), little to no Rtls signal was detected by immunofluorescence when wild-type single cells and chains were imaged with the settings used for visualizing Rtls in rosettes (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: S. rosetta chain colonies and single cells may release Rtls into their aquatic environment, where it may be washed away during processing of cells for immunofluorescence.
source: Because Rtls has a predicted secretion signal, it is possible that S. rosetta chain colonies and single cells released Rtls into their aquatic environment, where it may have been washed away during processing of cells for immunofluorescence.
evidence: Speculation based on the presence of a signal peptide and differential detection of Rtls in different cell types.

claim: After increasing the gain used during confocal imaging, Rtls was detected in cell membrane-associated patches in wild-type single cells and chains.
source: After increasing the gain used during confocal imaging, we were able to detect Rtls in cell membrane-associated patches in wild-type single cells and chains, but these patches were absent from Rosetteless mutant cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Rtls patches were absent from Rosetteless mutant cells.
source: After increasing the gain used during confocal imaging, we were able to detect Rtls in cell membrane-associated patches in wild-type single cells and chains, but these patches were absent from Rosetteless mutant cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The patches of Rtls localization were most often located near the basal pole of each cell.
source: The patches of Rtls localization were most often located near the basal pole of each cell, but were sometimes detected at the apical pole or along the lateral regions of the cell (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Rtls staining in single cells or chains was never as intense as the Rtls staining observed in the cores of rosettes.
source: In no case was the Rtls staining in single cells or chains as intense as the Rtls staining observed in the cores of rosettes.
evidence: Comparison of immunofluorescence intensity across different cell types shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The localization of Rtls protein is developmentally regulated and most abundant in the core of rosettes.
source: In summary, three findings demonstrate that Rtls function is necessary for and specific to rosette development: (1) the localization of Rtls protein is developmentally regulated and most abundant in the core of rosettes, (2) Rosetteless mutant cells fail to form rosettes but are otherwise wild type, and (3) secreted Rtls protein is essential for rosette development, while being dispensable during other stages of the S. rosetta life history.
evidence: Summary of immunofluorescence data showing differential Rtls localization.

claim: Rosetteless mutant cells fail to form rosettes but are otherwise wild type.
source: In summary, three findings demonstrate that Rtls function is necessary for and specific to rosette development: (1) the localization of Rtls protein is developmentally regulated and most abundant in the core of rosettes, (2) Rosetteless mutant cells fail to form rosettes but are otherwise wild type, and (3) secreted Rtls protein is essential for rosette development, while being dispensable during other stages of the S. rosetta life history.
evidence: Summary of phenotypic characterization data.

claim: Secreted Rtls protein is essential for rosette development, while being dispensable during other stages of the S. rosetta life history.
source: In summary, three findings demonstrate that Rtls function is necessary for and specific to rosette development: (1) the localization of Rtls protein is developmentally regulated and most abundant in the core of rosettes, (2) Rosetteless mutant cells fail to form rosettes but are otherwise wild type, and (3) secreted Rtls protein is essential for rosette development, while being dispensable during other stages of the S. rosetta life history.
evidence: Summary of antibody blocking experiments and phenotypic characterization.

claim: The rosetteless gene is the only gene yet known to be required for choanoflagellate multicellular development.
source: The rosetteless gene is the only gene yet known to be required for choanoflagellate multicellular development.
evidence: Statement of the novelty of this finding in the context of choanoflagellate research.

claim: Rtls may stabilize the connections between rosette cells by interacting with the ECM in a manner akin to the lecticans.
source: Rtls may stabilize the connections between rosette cells by interacting with the ECM in a manner akin to the lecticans, a family of animal C-type lectins that stabilize cartilage and other connective tissues by cross-linking carbohydrates and proteins in the ECM (Ruoslahti, 1996).
evidence: Speculation based on Rtls localization and comparison to animal lectican function.

claim: Lecticans are a family of animal C-type lectins that stabilize cartilage and other connective tissues by cross-linking carbohydrates and proteins in the ECM.
source: Rtls may stabilize the connections between rosette cells by interacting with the ECM in a manner akin to the lecticans, a family of animal C-type lectins that stabilize cartilage and other connective tissues by cross-linking carbohydrates and proteins in the ECM (Ruoslahti, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on lectican function.

claim: One of the main differences between rosettes and chain colonies lies in the stability and mechanical robustness of rosettes as compared to chain colonies.
source: Such a role would be consistent with the observation that the Rosetteless mutant produces wild-type chain colonies, as one of the main differences between rosettes and chain colonies lies in the stability and mechanical robustness of rosettes as compared to chain colonies.
evidence: Inference based on phenotypic observations of rosettes and chain colonies.

claim: The Rtls CTLDs most closely resemble animal CTLDs that preferentially bind mannose, such as mannose binding protein and pulmonary surfactant protein A.
source: A second possible hint regarding Rtls function stems from the fact that the Rtls CTLDs most closely resemble animal CTLDs that preferentially bind mannose (Drickamer, 1992), such as mannose binding protein and pulmonary surfactant protein A, each of which functions in innate immunity as pattern recognition receptors (Takahashi et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference based on sequence similarity and citation to literature on mannose-binding CTLDs.

claim: Mannose binding protein and pulmonary surfactant protein A each function in innate immunity as pattern recognition receptors.
source: A second possible hint regarding Rtls function stems from the fact that the Rtls CTLDs most closely resemble animal CTLDs that preferentially bind mannose (Drickamer, 1992), such as mannose binding protein and pulmonary surfactant protein A, each of which functions in innate immunity as pattern recognition receptors (Takahashi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on these proteins.

claim: Rtls may play a role in substrate recognition and cell signaling.
source: Because rosette development is regulated by bacterial signals (Alegado et al., 2012), Rtls may play a role in substrate recognition and cell signaling.
evidence: Speculation based on bacterial regulation of rosette development and similarity to pattern recognition receptors.

claim: CTLD-containing proteins have been shown to regulate cell adhesion and development in animals.
source: CTLD-containing proteins have previously been shown to regulate cell adhesion and development in animals (Reidling et al., 2000; Iba et al., 2001; Kulkarni et al., 2008; Chin and Mlodzik, 2013), offering intriguing parallels with the role of the Rosetteless CTLD protein in the control of rosette development.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on CTLD protein functions in animals.

claim: The genomes of diverse animals encode Rtls-like proteins containing a signal peptide, two C-type lectin-like domains, and serine-threonine-rich low complexity regions.
source: Moreover, while the genomes of diverse animals encode Rtls-like proteins containing a signal peptide, two C-type lectin-like domains, and serine-threonine-rich low complexity regions (e.g., the placozoan Trichoplax adhaerans (XP_002112548), the cnidarian Hydra vulgaris (XP_002155329), the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (NP_501369.1), and the fish Danio rerio (XP_005158004); relevant motifs detected by SMART, [Letunic et al., 2012]), it is not clear whether the similarities among these proteins and Rtls are the result of homology or convergent evolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis of animal genomes with specific protein accession numbers provided.

claim: It is not clear whether the similarities among animal Rtls-like proteins and Rtls are the result of homology or convergent evolution.
source: Moreover, while the genomes of diverse animals encode Rtls-like proteins containing a signal peptide, two C-type lectin-like domains, and serine-threonine-rich low complexity regions (e.g., the placozoan Trichoplax adhaerans (XP_002112548), the cnidarian Hydra vulgaris (XP_002155329), the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (NP_501369.1), and the fish Danio rerio (XP_005158004); relevant motifs detected by SMART, [Letunic et al., 2012]), it is not clear whether the similarities among these proteins and Rtls are the result of homology or convergent evolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inference based on difficulty in establishing orthology relationships for CTLD-containing proteins.

claim: Forward genetic screens have been vital tools for uncovering fundamental mechanisms driving development in eukaryotic model organisms.
source: Forward genetic screens have been vital tools for uncovering fundamental mechanisms driving development in eukaryotic model organisms, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Drosophila melanogaster, C. elegans, Mus musculus, D. rerio, and Arabidopsis thaliana (Hartwell et al., 1970; Brenner, 1974; Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus, 1980; Mayer et al., 1991; Haffter et al., 1996; Kasarskis et al., 1998), but such approaches have been restricted to a relatively small number of taxa that represent a small fraction of eukaryotic diversity (Abzhanov et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to landmark forward genetic studies.

claim: Forward genetic approaches have been restricted to a relatively small number of taxa that represent a small fraction of eukaryotic diversity.
source: Forward genetic screens have been vital tools for uncovering fundamental mechanisms driving development in eukaryotic model organisms, including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Drosophila melanogaster, C. elegans, Mus musculus, D. rerio, and Arabidopsis thaliana (Hartwell et al., 1970; Brenner, 1974; Nüsslein-Volhard and Wieschaus, 1980; Mayer et al., 1991; Haffter et al., 1996; Kasarskis et al., 1998), but such approaches have been restricted to a relatively small number of taxa that represent a small fraction of eukaryotic diversity (Abzhanov et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation discussing the limited phylogenetic breadth of model organisms.

claim: The establishment of forward genetics in choanoflagellates has provided the first insights into the genetic underpinnings of development in these evolutionarily relevant organisms.
source: The establishment of forward genetics in choanoflagellates has provided the first insights into the genetic underpinnings of development in these evolutionarily relevant organisms and promises to illuminate mechanisms underlying intercellular interactions in the progenitors of animals.
evidence: Summary statement of the significance of this study.

claim: S. rosetta cells have a single apical flagellum encircled by a collar of microvilli.
source: S. rosetta cells are polarized, each having a single apical flagellum encircled by a collar of microvilli (bracket), shown in cross-sectional diagram (A) and through DIC imaging of a live cell (B).
evidence: Diagram and microscopy image shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In rosette colonies, each cell is oriented around a central point, with the flagella facing outward.
source: In rosette colonies (C), each cell is oriented around a central point, with the flagella facing outward.
evidence: Microscopy image shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Bacterial prey attach transiently to the collars of some cells prior to ingestion by phagocytosis.
source: Bacterial prey (∼1 µm rods) attach transiently to the collars of some cells prior to ingestion by phagocytosis.
evidence: Observation described in text and visible in Figure 1.

claim: S. rosetta transitions between several morphologically differentiated cell types during its life history: rosette colonies, chain colonies, slow swimmers, fast swimmers, and thecate cells.
source: S. rosetta transitions between several morphologically differentiated cell types during its life history: rosette colonies (RC), chain colonies (CC), slow swimmers (SS), fast swimmers (FS), and thecate cells (TC).
evidence: Life cycle diagram shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The transition from slow swimmers to rosette colonies is induced by lipids from the bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis and can be regulated in the laboratory.
source: The transition from slow swimmers to rosette colonies (star) is induced by lipids from the bacterium Algoriphagus machipongonensis and can be regulated in the laboratory.
evidence: Life cycle diagram shown in Figure 1D with citation to previous work.

claim: S. rosetta undergoes a sexual cycle in the laboratory.
source: S. rosetta undergoes a sexual cycle in the laboratory.
evidence: Sexual cycle diagram shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When starved, haploid S. rosetta cultures produce anisogamous gametes that are capable of mating to produce diploids.
source: When starved, haploid cultures produce anisogamous gametes that are capable of mating to produce diploids.
evidence: Sexual cycle diagram shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Diploids undergo meiosis and thereby produce haploids when grown in nutrient-rich media.
source: Diploids undergo meiosis and thereby produce haploids when grown in nutrient-rich media.
evidence: Sexual cycle diagram shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Haploids and diploids can reproduce asexually through mitosis.
source: Haploids and diploids can also reproduce asexually through mitosis.
evidence: Sexual cycle diagram shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most markers followed Mendel's law of Segregation and Independent Assortment in the S. rosetta mapping cross.
source: Genotyping of each haploid isolate at 60 polymorphic sites across the genome revealed that most markers followed Mendel's law of Segregation and Independent Assortment ('Materials and methods', Figure 4—source data 1) (Mendel, 1866); thus S. rosetta inheritance appears to follow the rules of classical genetics.
evidence: Genotyping data from the mapping cross demonstrating expected segregation patterns.

claim: S. rosetta inheritance appears to follow the rules of classical genetics.
source: Genotyping of each haploid isolate at 60 polymorphic sites across the genome revealed that most markers followed Mendel's law of Segregation and Independent Assortment ('Materials and methods', Figure 4—source data 1) (Mendel, 1866); thus S. rosetta inheritance appears to follow the rules of classical genetics.
evidence: Inference based on observed Mendelian segregation patterns in the mapping cross.

claim: The mapping cross allowed for the generation of a linkage map containing 27 preliminary linkage groups that represent approximately 70% of the S. rosetta genome.
source: Analysis of the genotyping data in haploids also revealed genetic linkage among some of the markers, allowing us to generate a linkage map containing 27 preliminary linkage groups that represent approximately 70% of the S. rosetta genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Linkage map shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rosette colonies and chain colonies have some similarities, including the presence of fine intercellular bridges connecting neighboring cells and similar transcriptional profiles.
source: Nonetheless, chain colonies and rosettes have some similarities, including the presence of fine intercellular bridges connecting neighboring cells and similar transcriptional profiles (Dayel et al., 2011; Fairclough et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The connections among cells in rosettes are robust and resistant to mechanical shear.
source: In addition to the differences in their morphology, the connections among cells in rosettes are robust and resistant to mechanical shear, whereas chain colonies are fragile and readily fall apart into individual cells when exposed to shear forces.
evidence: Phenotypic observation used to distinguish rosettes from chain colonies.
